entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ursicinus, also known as Ursinus, emerged as a central figure in one of the most violent and politically charged papal elections in Roman history, occurring in 366 CE. His election as Bishop of Rome challenged the legitimacy of Damasus I, leading to a schism that exposed deep divisions within the nascent Christian Church and the Roman aristocracy. This struggle for the papacy, fueled by theological disputes, personal rivalries, and imperial interference, underscored the growing temporal power of the Roman bishopric in the late Roman Empire and the critical role of imperial patronage in ecclesiastical affairs.

Following the death of Pope Liberius in September 366, two factions within the Roman clergy and populace quickly nominated rival candidates. Ursicinus was elected by a group of deacons and laypeople, primarily those who had remained loyal to Liberius during his exile under Emperor Constantius II, and consecrated in the Basilica Julia. Simultaneously, the opposing faction, supported by many of Rome's aristocratic families and a more conservative clergy, elected Damasus I in the Basilica of Lucina. The ensuing conflict escalated into open street warfare, resulting in numerous deaths, notably a massacre at the Basilica of Sicininus (modern Santa Maria Maggiore) where 137 bodies were reportedly found. Emperor Valentinian I initially exiled Ursicinus but later allowed him to return, though the political maneuvering ultimately favored Damasus, who secured imperial recognition.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ursicinus's violent challenge to Damasus I in 366 CE exposed deep divisions within the Roman Church and aristocracy, leading to a bloody schism and establishing a precedent for imperial intervention in papal elections. This event underscored the growing temporal power of the papacy and the political complexities of its early development, influencing the understanding of legitimate authority within the Church.
